Actions on Objectives

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SprySOCKS (FishMonger/I-SOON) C2 beacon to hardcoded Vultr IPs 207.148.78.36 / 207.148.75.122 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SprySOCKS (FishMonger/I-SOON) C2 beacon to hardcoded Vultr IPs 207.148.78.36 / 207.148.75.122 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the two hardcoded SprySOCKS infrastructure IPs ESET attributed to FishMonger: WIN_PLUS C&C 207.148.78.36 (TCP/UDP/WebSocket on 443/53/80) and delivery server 207.148.75.122. These are hard IOCs confirmed by multiple vendors, so any egress to them is high-fidelity regardless of the initiating binary (the WIN_DRV variant diverts C2 over a random TCP port, so do not pin on a fixed listening port). Rationale: Uses the two ESET-published hardcoded IPs (207.148.78.36 C&C and 207.148.75.122 delivery server), each confirmed by Security Affairs and gbhackers. Matching on exact IP rather than the broader shared Vultr /20 keeps FP near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://securityaffairs.com/193728/apt/china-linked-fishmonger-ports-sprysocks-to-windows-with-kernel-level-stealth-and-uefi-bootkit-hints.html • https://gbhackers.com/sprysocks-windows-backdoor-uses-kernel/
ATT&CKT1071 T1095 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A different, benign tenant workload legitimately rents the same recycled Vultr IP after the campaign infrastructure was torn down (Vultr IPs are reassigned)
  • Security researcher / sandbox detonation host in your environment deliberately contacting the IOC
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling or IOC-validation scanner probing the address
  • NAT/proxy egress IP making the source attribution ambiguous (confirm the real internal host)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal host and the InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA1 making the connection; pull the process tree and check whether the binary SHA1 matches the SprySOCKS hash list (UC2). 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block 207.148.78.36, 207.148.75.122 and review the wider 207.148.64.0/20 Vultr range at the perimeter; preserve memory for the kernel-driver rootkit. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for unsigned/hidden kernel driver loads, hidden listening ports, EFI System Partition tampering (UC3), and any other host beaconing to the same /20.

SprySOCKS WIN_DRV/WIN_PLUS backdoor binary by ESET SHA1 hash AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution, file write, or image load of any of the 11 SprySOCKS Windows binaries (WIN_DRV / WIN_PLUS variants and loaders) by their ESET-published SHA1 hashes. WIN_DRV ships a kernel driver that hides its own processes, files, registry keys and network connections, so on-host hash matching at write/load time is the most reliable surface before the rootkit engages. Rationale: All 11 SHA1 values are the ESET-published SprySOCKS sample hashes from the article IOC block, cross-checked against the ESET blog mirror and Security Affairs. Hash matching is exact and survives the rootkit's process/file hiding because it fires at write/load time. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://www.esetngblog.com/post/fishmonger-s-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-for-windows • https://securityaffairs.com/193728/apt/china-linked-fishmonger-ports-sprysocks-to-windows-with-kernel-level-stealth-and-uefi-bootkit-hints.html
ATT&CKT1014 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV/EDR quarantine copies or VirusTotal-uploaded sample handling on an analyst/sandbox host re-surfacing the same hash
  • Threat-intel platform storing the sample on disk during enrichment
  • Re-used hash from a generic packer producing a benign-file collision (extremely unlikely for SHA1, but verify file path/signer)
  • Purple-team or detection-validation exercise intentionally dropping the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hit is on a production endpoint (not a sandbox/IR jump box); capture FolderPath, signer, and the InitiatingProcess that wrote/loaded it. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, collect a memory image before the kernel driver can re-hide artifacts, and submit the binary for analysis. 3) Hunt: search the org for any of the other 10 hashes, for connections to the UC1 C2 IPs, for service installations and EFI/boot tampering (UC3), and scope FishMonger lateral movement to other government/high-value hosts.

SprySOCKS WIN_DRV BlackLotus-style Secure Boot downgrade / EFI bootkit (CVE-2023-24932) AIInstallation Low
Hunts for the UEFI bootkit component ESET reports as a 'limited indication' in some SprySOCKS attacks: a CVE-2023-24932 BlackLotus-style downgrade that writes a revoked/older boot manager (bootmgfw.efi/bootmgr.efi/bootx64.efi) onto the EFI System Partition. Flags .efi writes to boot paths by processes other than the Windows servicing stack — the EDR-blind firmware persistence this campaign may layer on top of the kernel rootkit. Rationale: Targets the article's CVE-2023-24932 UEFI bootkit lead by detecting the BlackLotus-style core action — writing a (revoked/downgraded) boot manager to the EFI System Partition — excluding the Windows servicing stack that legitimately updates these files. Confidence is Low because ESET itself frames the bootkit as a 'limited indication'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/fishmongers-arsenal-upgraded-sprysocks-windows/ • https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/how-to-manage-the-windows-boot-manager-revocations-for-secure-boot-changes-associated-with-cve-2023-24932-41a975df-beb2-40c1-99a3-b3ff139f832d • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/vulnerabilities/cve-2023-24932
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1553.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Windows cumulative/feature update or KB5025885 Secure Boot servicing applying the boot manager (TrustedInstaller/TiWorker — filtered, but third-party servicing tools may not be)
  • OEM/IT imaging and BCD repair via bcdboot.exe / dism during provisioning
  • BitLocker recovery or bootrec /rebuildbcd troubleshooting by a sysadmin
  • Endpoint backup/restore agents touching the ESP
  • Dual-boot or Linux bootloader (e.g. shim/grub) installation writing .efi files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("bcdboot.exe","dism.exe","setuphost.exe","reagentc.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows\WinSxS\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and its signer; confirm whether it is a sanctioned servicing/imaging tool and whether the dropped .efi is Microsoft-signed and current (compare hash/version against a known-good). 2) Contain: if non-servicing, isolate the host, verify Secure Boot state and DBX revocation status, and treat as firmware-level compromise — reimage may be insufficient; rebuild the ESP from trusted media. 3) Hunt: correlate the host with UC1 C2 beacons and UC2 SprySOCKS hashes, review for Memory Integrity/HVCI or BitLocker being disabled, unrecognized .efi files, BCD edits, and apply CVE-2023-24932 DBX revocations fleet-wide.

| where FileName in~ ("bootmgfw.efi","bootmgr.efi","bootx64.efi") or FolderPath has @"\EFI\" or FolderPath has "HarddiskVolume"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("TiWorker.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","poqexec.exe","MoUsoCoreWorker.exe","CompatTelRunner.exe","wuauclt.exe","setup.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| where ActingProcessName !has "TrustedInstaller.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "TiWorker.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "poqexec.exe" and ActingProcessName !has "CompatTelRunner.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, DvcAction, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-24932")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.

        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("955BFC3DCC867256F9F46A606DEB0779FA3416D8", "44DC4A08C5EB0972C8E18B0E01284E06F09006BB", "AB87B29B6F79487C75CA08D102E79001E536F083", "6490B8E4AADE25A3EE2DA9A47F312DB2122470BC", "E7484C24B88A1A2407A8F09D734F9A993670285B", "621D1952839BE4B0A1B0E66E87BCE5062CA368ED", "2457EED2AB28E37741F10914EF929DAD2C8079D4", "D2C706B1EAF662BF0CE124B5032F73ED84BDA24A", "5F3B87CEF56683D9A9E19186E0FD0D8019B559C4", "C793CA31E3F6628B5C8986146953BF66232E9A30", "037DB2445F3D72388CB2CF8510563148E5A184BE") or SHA1 in~ ("955BFC3DCC867256F9F46A606DEB0779FA3416D8", "44DC4A08C5EB0972C8E18B0E01284E06F09006BB", "AB87B29B6F79487C75CA08D102E79001E536F083", "6490B8E4AADE25A3EE2DA9A47F312DB2122470BC", "E7484C24B88A1A2407A8F09D734F9A993670285B", "621D1952839BE4B0A1B0E66E87BCE5062CA368ED", "2457EED2AB28E37741F10914EF929DAD2C8079D4", "D2C706B1EAF662BF0CE124B5032F73ED84BDA24A", "5F3B87CEF56683D9A9E19186E0FD0D8019B559C4", "C793CA31E3F6628B5C8986146953BF66232E9A30", "037DB2445F3D72388CB2CF8510563148E5A184BE") or MD5 in~ ("955BFC3DCC867256F9F46A606DEB0779FA3416D8", "44DC4A08C5EB0972C8E18B0E01284E06F09006BB", "AB87B29B6F79487C75CA08D102E79001E536F083", "6490B8E4AADE25A3EE2DA9A47F312DB2122470BC", "E7484C24B88A1A2407A8F09D734F9A993670285B", "621D1952839BE4B0A1B0E66E87BCE5062CA368ED", "2457EED2AB28E37741F10914EF929DAD2C8079D4", "D2C706B1EAF662BF0CE124B5032F73ED84BDA24A", "5F3B87CEF56683D9A9E19186E0FD0D8019B559C4", "C793CA31E3F6628B5C8986146953BF66232E9A30", "037DB2445F3D72388CB2CF8510563148E5A184BE")

| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["955BFC3DCC867256F9F46A606DEB0779FA3416D8", "44DC4A08C5EB0972C8E18B0E01284E06F09006BB", "AB87B29B6F79487C75CA08D102E79001E536F083", "6490B8E4AADE25A3EE2DA9A47F312DB2122470BC", "E7484C24B88A1A2407A8F09D734F9A993670285B", "621D1952839BE4B0A1B0E66E87BCE5062CA368ED", "2457EED2AB28E37741F10914EF929DAD2C8079D4", "D2C706B1EAF662BF0CE124B5032F73ED84BDA24A", "5F3B87CEF56683D9A9E19186E0FD0D8019B559C4", "C793CA31E3F6628B5C8986146953BF66232E9A30", "037DB2445F3D72388CB2CF8510563148E5A184BE"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has

// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48907")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")

| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser/Playwright process overwriting vite.config / vitest.config (CVE-2026-53633) AIInstallation High
Hunts the verified impact of CVE-2026-53633: a CDP-driven browser download writes attacker-controlled vite.config.ts into the project root, which Vitest then reloads as Node.js code. A Chromium/Playwright browser binary creating or modifying a build/test config file is essentially never legitimate, making this the highest-fidelity pivot for the exploit. Rationale: Keys on the exact verified impact chain in the GHSA: a CDP Page.setDownloadBehavior + Runtime.evaluate download writing vite.config.ts to project root, with a browser binary (incl. Playwright's headless_shell/chrome) as the writer. Excluding the user Downloads folder removes the only benign way a browser legitimately writes such a name. Cross-checked against the upstream vitest advisory and GitLab Advisory DB. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@vitest/browser/CVE-2026-53633/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team reproducing CVE-2026-53633 in a sandbox
  • Vitest's own browser-mode self-tests running in a CI image where the test harness is a browser
  • Developer doing browser 'Save As' of a file literally named vite.config.ts into a repo (mitigated by Downloads exclusion)
  • A browser-embedded local IDE/extension that persists project files through the renderer process
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "ms-playwright" or FolderPath !contains "\\node_modules\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writer is a real browser/Playwright binary and the target is a tracked project config; diff the new vite.config content for require/child_process/exec/fetch or base64 blobs. 2) Contain: kill the Vitest watch (node) and browser sessions on the host, isolate the endpoint, and revert vite.config from version control. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for node.exe children spawned within 60s of the write (UC2), inbound connections to the Vitest listener (UC4), and any `--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0` invocations (UC3).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("vite.config.ts","vite.config.js","vite.config.mjs","vite.config.mts","vite.config.cjs","vitest.config.ts","vitest.config.js","vitest.config.mjs","vitest.config.mts")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","headless_shell.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
| where FolderPath !contains "\\Downloads\\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileOriginUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("vite.config.ts","vite.config.js","vite.config.mjs","vite.config.mts","vite.config.cjs","vitest.config.ts","vitest.config.js","vitest.config.mjs","vitest.config.mts")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","headless_shell.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
| where TargetFilePath !contains "\\Downloads\\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Browser Process Overwriting Vite/Vitest Config File (CVE-2026-53633)
id: 6f3a1b2c-9d4e-4a77-bf21-7c1e5a9d0e11
description: A Chromium/Playwright browser binary writing a vite.config or vitest.config file indicates abuse of the Vitest Browser Mode CDP bridge (CVE-2026-53633) to overwrite project config and gain Node.js RCE.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
  - https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.t1546
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\chromium.exe'
      - '\headless_shell.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
  selection_file:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\vite.config.ts'
      - '\vite.config.js'
      - '\vite.config.mjs'
      - '\vite.config.mts'
      - '\vite.config.cjs'
      - '\vitest.config.ts'
      - '\vitest.config.js'
      - '\vitest.config.mjs'
  filter_downloads:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\Downloads\'
  condition: selection_img and selection_file and not filter_downloads
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\chromium.exe OR *\headless_shell.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\firefox.exe OR *\brave.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\vite.config.ts OR *\vite.config.js OR *\vite.config.mjs OR *\vitest.config.ts OR *\vitest.config.js) -@TargetFilename:*\Downloads\*
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\(vite|vitest)\.config\.(ts|js|mjs|mts|cjs)$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|chromium|headless_shell|msedge|firefox|brave)\.exe$/i
| NOT (TargetFileName=/\\Downloads\\/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Vitest config overwrite by browser followed by Node child execution (CVE-2026-53633 RCE) AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates the CVE-2026-53633 config overwrite with the resulting code execution: a browser binary writes vite.config/vitest.config, then the running Vitest node process spawns a child process within seconds as the reloaded, attacker-controlled config executes. The temporal link between a browser-written config and node-spawned children is the proof of RCE, not just exposure. Rationale: Joins the article's two-step chain — browser writes vite.config (CDP download) then 'Vitest reloads the changed config and executes attacker-controlled Node.js code' — by requiring a node/vitest-parented child process within 60s of a browser-written config on the same host. The browser-writer + node-parent combo within seconds is what separates exploitation from benign config edits. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
ATT&CKT1546 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Vitest watch reload after a developer edits config in a browser-based local IDE
  • CVE reproduction/red-team exercise on a dev box
  • Vitest self-tests in CI that intentionally rewrite config during a run
  • A browser extension that round-trips project files then triggers a vite HMR reload
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "esbuild" and ProcessCommandLine !has "--version"
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the spawned child cmdline (DelaySec near 0 = automated) and the new config content for malicious Node payloads. 2) Contain: terminate the node/vitest watcher and child processes, isolate the host, restore config from VCS, and rotate any secrets reachable from the project (.env, npm tokens). 3) Hunt: enumerate outbound connections and files created by the child process, and sweep other dev endpoints for `--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0` Vitest listeners (UC3).

    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","headless_shell.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
    | project ConfigWriteTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ConfigFile = FileName, ConfigPath = FolderPath, WriterProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("vitest","vite")
| join kind=inner ConfigWrites on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (ConfigWriteTime .. ConfigWriteTime + WindowSeconds * 1s)
| project ConfigWriteTime, ReexecTime = Timestamp, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ConfigWriteTime), DeviceName, ConfigFile, ConfigPath, WriterProcess, ChildProcess = FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by ConfigWriteTime desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let WindowSeconds = 60;
let ConfigWrites = ImFileEvent

    | where TargetFileName in~ ("vite.config.ts","vite.config.js","vite.config.mjs","vite.config.mts","vite.config.cjs","vitest.config.ts","vitest.config.js","vitest.config.mjs")
    | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","headless_shell.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
    | project ConfigWriteTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ConfigFile = TargetFileName, WriterProcess = ActingProcessName;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ParentProcessName has "node.exe"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("vitest","vite")
| join kind=inner ConfigWrites on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (ConfigWriteTime .. ConfigWriteTime + WindowSeconds * 1s)
| project ConfigWriteTime, ReexecTime = TimeGenerated, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, ConfigWriteTime), DvcHostname, ConfigFile, WriterProcess, ChildProcess = ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by ConfigWriteTime desc

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, TargetFileName], function=count())

Vitest Browser Mode API exposed to all interfaces (--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0) AIDelivery Medium
Identifies the precise dangerous configuration enabling remote exploitation of CVE-2026-53633: a Vitest/node process started with the browser API bound to 0.0.0.0. The query also surfaces whether allowWrite/allowExec are disabled — the 'false sense of security' the advisory calls out, since CDP bypasses those flags regardless. Rationale: Uses the exact CLI string the advisory's Impact section names ('--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0') as the condition that turns the local CDP bypass into a remote RCE, and flags the allowWrite/allowExec=false combination the article explicitly calls out as a false sense of security. This is a posture hunt, hence hunting tier — it finds exposure, not confirmed compromise. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@vitest/browser/CVE-2026-53633/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/container runners intentionally binding 0.0.0.0 inside an isolated network
  • Developers running Vitest UI to share a test session with a teammate on the LAN
  • Cloud dev environments (Codespaces/Gitpod) that bind 0.0.0.0 by design
  • Security team validating the patched 3.2.5/4.1.8/5.0.0-beta.4 behavior
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !startswith "ci-" and DeviceName !startswith "runner-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host runs a vulnerable @vitest/browser (>=3.0.0<=3.2.4, >=4.0.0<=4.1.7, 5.0.0-beta.0..3) or vite-plus<=0.1.23 and whether the API is reachable off-host. 2) Contain: stop the exposed Vitest watcher, restrict the API to 127.0.0.1, and upgrade to 3.2.5 / 4.1.8 / 5.0.0-beta.4+. 3) Hunt: check for inbound connections to the listener (UC4) and any browser-written config files (UC1) on this host during the exposure window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","vitest.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "vitest"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0","--browser.api.host 0.0.0.0","--api.host=0.0.0.0","--api.host 0.0.0.0")
| extend WriteExecDisabled = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("allowWrite=false","allowWrite false","allowExec=false","allowExec false")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, WriteExecDisabled, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","vitest.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "vitest"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0","--browser.api.host 0.0.0.0","--api.host=0.0.0.0","--api.host 0.0.0.0")
| extend WriteExecDisabled = ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("allowWrite=false","allowExec=false")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, WriteExecDisabled
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote inbound connection to Vitest Browser Mode listener (node, non-loopback) AIExploitation Medium
Detects a remote client reaching an exposed Vitest browser API: the node/vitest process accepts an inbound connection from a non-loopback address. Remote exploitation of CVE-2026-53633 requires connecting to the WebSocket API (default port 63315) to scrape the API token/session and issue CDP RPC, so a non-local inbound to the vitest listener is the network signature of the attack. Rationale: Pins the Defender query to the reliable signal (a vitest-cmdline node process accepting a non-loopback inbound), and uses the article's stated listener port 63315 where process attribution isn't available (Datadog/Falcon). Sentinel left empty because the standard ASIM/SecurityEvent tables in this tenant carry no inbound-connection record attributable to the listening node/vitest process — explained per the schema's process-attribution gap. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Teammates on the LAN connecting to a shared Vitest UI / dev server
  • Mobile or VM browsers hitting the dev server for cross-device testing
  • Internal vulnerability scanners or asset-discovery probes touching the port
  • Monitoring/health-check agents connecting to the node listener
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("<populate with known dev/monitoring subnets via watchlist>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the RemoteIP — is it a known dev/teammate host or unexpected/external? Correlate the connection time with any browser-written config (UC1) on the same host. 2) Contain: if unexpected, isolate the host, kill the Vitest watcher, and block the source IP; rebind the API to localhost. 3) Hunt: review the source IP's activity org-wide and check the target host for node-spawned child processes and new config files post-connection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "vitest"
| where RemoteIPType !in ("Loopback","LinkLocal")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "vitest"
| where RemoteIPType !in ("Loopback","LinkLocal")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| NOT (RemoteAddressIP4=/^127\./ OR RemoteAddressIP4="::1")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, LocalPort, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] EvilTokens device-code token polling from attacker infra (python-requests UA / C2 IPs) · [LLM] EvilTokens device-code lure email (Acrobat/DocuSign decoy, 'Verify to view') · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Microsoft 365 OAuth device code authentication flow sign-in (EvilTokens) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Post-device-code malicious inbox rule creation (BEC prep) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Microsoft 365 OAuth device code authentication flow sign-in (EvilTokens) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces successful Entra ID sign-ins that completed via the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant flow — the exact mechanism EvilTokens abuses to have a victim authorize the attacker's session on the genuine microsoft.com/devicelogin page. In tenants that don't legitimately use device code flow, any occurrence is a strong account-takeover indicator. Rationale: Anchors on the OAuth device code grant — the single behaviour that defines EvilTokens — surfaced via the AuthenticationProcessingDetails 'Device Code' marker (Defender/Sentinel) and AuthenticationProtocol=deviceCode (Sigma). Microsoft and Sekoia both confirm deviceCode/originalTransferMethod fields are the primary detection surface and are absent from normal interactive sign-ins. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-oauth-device-code-phishing-m365-20260325-c/
ATT&CKT1528 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running 'az login --use-device-code' from a workstation
  • Sysadmin connecting Microsoft Graph PowerShell with -UseDeviceAuthentication
  • Conference-room / smart-TV / kiosk device enrollment using device code
  • Legacy line-of-business app onboarded via device code grant
  • Help-desk provisioning a shared device on behalf of a user
Suppression filter
| where tostring(parse_json(tostring(DeviceDetail)).trustType) !in ("Azure AD joined", "Hybrid Azure AD joined")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the sign-in's IPAddress, UserAgent, AppDisplayName and DeviceTrust. Managed/compliant device + corporate IP + Azure CLI/PowerShell app = likely admin self-service; unmanaged device + VPS/residential-proxy IP + python-requests UA = treat as compromise. 2) Contain: if suspicious, revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset, and require re-MFA. 3) Hunt: review the same user's subsequent mailbox access, new inbox rules, OneDrive/SharePoint downloads, and any Teams/Graph activity from the same IP in the following 72h.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
| extend DeviceTrust = tostring(parse_json(tostring(DeviceDetail)).trustType)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, DeviceTrust, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EvilTokens device-code token polling from attacker infra (python-requests UA / C2 IPs) AIDelivery Medium
Detects device-code sign-ins originating from the EvilTokens C2 IP ranges or carrying the python-requests user-agent characteristic of the kit's token-polling loop against Microsoft's devicecode endpoint. This is the attacker's authenticating 'device' picking up access/refresh tokens after the victim enters the code. Rationale: Combines the corroborated device-code protocol with two high-fidelity discriminators: the python-requests token-polling user-agent (named in Microsoft's Storm-2372 analysis) and the article's EvilTokens IP ranges (treated as /24 from the .0 IOCs). The TTP+UA pair is cross-confirmed; the specific IPs are article-sourced enrichment. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1078.004 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal Python automation/script using device code flow against Graph (uncommon)
  • Security scanner or red-team tooling emulating device code phishing
  • Shared NAT egress where a single corporate IP overlaps a flagged hosting range (unlikely for the listed VPS blocks)
  • Pen-test of conditional access device-code policy
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the AccountUpn, the AppDisplayName the token was minted for, and whether the source IP is a known VPS/hosting block; python-requests + device code is effectively never benign for end-user accounts. 2) Contain: immediately revoke sessions and refresh tokens for the account, disable the account if active mailbox/Graph access is seen, and add the IP ranges to a block/Conditional-Access named location. 3) Hunt: sweep all other accounts that authenticated from the same IPs in the last 30 days, and pivot to OfficeActivity/CloudAppEvents for inbox-rule creation and mass downloads.

| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails contains "Device Code"
| where UserAgent has "python-requests"
    or ipv4_is_in_any_range(IPAddress, "162.220.232.0/24", "162.220.234.0/24", "89.150.45.0/24", "185.81.113.0/24")
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ErrorCode, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)

    or ipv4_is_in_any_range(IPAddress, "162.220.232.0/24", "162.220.234.0/24", "89.150.45.0/24", "185.81.113.0/24")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ResultType, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState

EvilTokens device-code lure email (Acrobat/DocuSign decoy, 'Verify to view') AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound mail delivering the EvilTokens lure — links to the kit's decoy domains or subjects impersonating document/signature/calendar requests that route the victim toward microsoft.com/devicelogin. Targets the delivery step before the victim ever enters the attacker's code. Rationale: Pivots on the kit's named decoy domains (authdocspro/docusend impersonating DocuSign, eventcalender-schedule for the calendar-invite lure) plus the article's verbatim lure strings 'Verify to view' / 'Signature required', combined with a devicelogin URL target. Domains are article-sourced; the Acrobat/DocuSign decoy theme is corroborated by Sekoia. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/cybercrime/eviltokens-phishing-doesnt-steal-password/
ATT&CKT1566.002
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine DocuSign/Adobe Acrobat Sign notification with a 'Signature required' subject
  • Legitimate SharePoint/OneDrive 'shared a document' invite
  • Internal calendar-invite tooling using 'Verify to access' language
  • Marketing/e-sign vendor newsletters that happen to contain the lure phrasing
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the sending domain's SPF/DKIM/DMARC and the UrlDomain reputation; a freshly-registered look-alike (authdocspro, docusend.networkssolutionmail) routing to devicelogin is high-confidence phishing. 2) Contain: ZAP/soft-delete the message across all recipients, block the sender + URL domains at the secure email gateway, and warn recipients not to enter any code. 3) Hunt: check UrlClickEvents for recipients who clicked, then correlate to SigninLogs for any device-code sign-in by those users within 15 minutes (the code's validity window).

Post-device-code malicious inbox rule creation (BEC prep) AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a recent device-code sign-in by a user with that same user creating an auto-delete/forward/move inbox rule — the EvilTokens post-compromise pattern where attackers hide replies and stage BEC. Ties two telemetry sources to cut the noise of routine rule changes. Rationale: Gates the well-known malicious-inbox-rule signal behind a recent device-code sign-in by the same identity, making it specific to the EvilTokens account-takeover chain rather than a generic rule-change hunt. The hide/forward parameter keywords match the article's 'new inbox rules' warning and corroborated BEC staging behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/cybercrime/eviltokens-phishing-doesnt-steal-password/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.003
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User who legitimately enrolled a device via device code then set up a normal folder-organization rule
  • Admin/help-desk creating delegate or archive rules on a mailbox
  • Outlook 'sweep'/clutter rule auto-moving newsletters to a folder
  • Legitimate auto-forward to a personal-archive mailbox approved by policy
Suppression filter
| where not (Parameters has "MoveToFolder" and Parameters !has_any ("ForwardTo", "RedirectTo", "DeleteMessage", "Deleted Items", "RSS Feeds"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the rule's Parameters/RawEventData — forwarding to an external address or moving replies to RSS Feeds/Deleted Items/Archive is hostile; benign rules sort known senders into named folders. 2) Contain: delete the malicious inbox rule, revoke the user's sessions/refresh tokens, reset credentials, and disable external auto-forwarding tenant-wide if not required. 3) Hunt: review Sent Items and OfficeActivity for outbound BEC messages, check whether finance/HR/AP counterparties were contacted, and pivot on the sign-in IP to find other compromised mailboxes.

| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, ActionType, ObjectName, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Tracing Digital Intent: New MacOS Tahoe 26 Artifact Discovered
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress

          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
