Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Budibase global-admin escalation via POST /api/public/v1/roles/assign (CVE-2026-48150) · [LLM] Budibase self-minted API key followed by global-role assignment (CVE-2026-48150 chain)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Budibase global-admin escalation via POST /api/public/v1/roles/assign (CVE-2026-48150) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP POSTs to Budibase's public-API roles/assign endpoint, the exact sink CVE-2026-48150 abuses to grant builder.global/admin.global to arbitrary user IDs. This endpoint is a niche Enterprise (EXPANDED_PUBLIC_API) surface; any POST to it on an unpatched (<3.39.0) tenant is worth a builder-role review since the HTTP layer cannot distinguish a legitimate global admin from an escalating workspace-scoped builder. Rationale: Uses the literal vulnerable endpoint path '/api/public/v1/roles/assign' + POST method from the advisory PoC; this public-API route is rarely called in normal operation, making method+path a high-signal pivot for the CVE-2026-48150 mass-assignment sink. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xp4-cf37-ppjh • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@budibase/server/CVE-2026-48150/ • https://docs.budibase.com/reference/roleassign • https://www.thehackerwire.com/budibase-critical-privilege-escalation-cve-2026-48150/
ATT&CKT1068 T1098
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate global admin using the public API / integration to assign or revoke roles in bulk
  • Automation or IaC pipeline that provisions Budibase users via the public API and calls roles/assign
  • Penetration-test or vulnerability-scanner traffic replaying the CVE PoC against the tenant
  • SCIM/SSO provisioning middleware that wraps the public roles endpoint
  • Internal QA/staging environment role seeding scripts
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.5")  // exclude known SSO/IaC provisioning host once identified during baselining
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: From the source IP/host, pull the Budibase identity behind the API key used (x-budibase-api-key) and confirm whether that caller already holds builder.global or admin.global. A caller who is only a workspace-scoped builder (builder.apps set, builder.global unset) = confirmed exploit. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the offending API key (regenerate via global self/api_key admin), reset the affected users' roles, and verify no user unexpectedly gained admin.global; upgrade the instance to Budibase 3.39.0+. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all userIds granted builder/admin global since the first POST, check for follow-on access to datasource credentials, SCIM/OIDC/audit-log config changes, and automation exports performed under the newly elevated identities.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| summarize Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Statuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode), UserAgents = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod
| order by LastSeen desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.status) as status values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/api/public/v1/roles/assign*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.status) as status values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/api/public/v1/roles/assign*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Budibase self-minted API key followed by global-role assignment (CVE-2026-48150 chain) AIExploitation Medium
Correlates a GET /api/global/self/api_key (the attacker minting an API key tied to their own identity) with a POST /api/public/v1/roles/assign from the same source within a short window — the exact two-step flow in the CVE-2026-48150 PoC where Alice mints a key then escalates herself/another user to global admin. Pairing the key-mint with the escalation removes most legitimate single-action noise. Rationale: Chains the two literal PoC paths ('/api/global/self/api_key' GET to mint, '/api/public/v1/roles/assign' POST to escalate) on the same source within 1h, matching the advisory's Step 2 to Step 3 attack flow; the temporal pairing is far higher fidelity than either request alone. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xp4-cf37-ppjh • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@budibase/server/CVE-2026-48150/ • https://docs.budibase.com/reference/roleassign
ATT&CKT1098 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An administrator legitimately generating a personal API key then using the public API to manage roles in one session
  • Onboarding automation that mints a service API key and immediately seeds user roles
  • Developer testing the public API end-to-end against a non-prod tenant
  • Shared egress NAT collapsing two different users (one minting a key, another assigning roles) to the same SrcIpAddr
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the Budibase user who minted the API key (GET self/api_key returns the userId) and check their pre-existing scope — a workspace-scoped builder minting a key then POSTing roles/assign is the confirmed CVE-2026-48150 chain. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke that API key, restore the affected users' original roles (note the SDK overwrites builder.apps scope, so re-apply scoping), and patch to 3.39.0+. 3) HUNT: Review all role grants from that identity, look for the follow-up 'admin:true' self-grant POST, and audit datasource/automation/SCIM access performed after the grant timestamp.
let window = 1h;
let keymint = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "/api/global/self/api_key"
    | project KeyMintTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| join kind=inner keymint on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (KeyMintTime .. KeyMintTime + window)  // key minted then used to escalate within 1h
| project KeyMintTime, AssignTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpStatusCode
| order by AssignTime desc
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Web.url) as urls min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/api/global/self/api_key*" OR Web.url="*/api/public/v1/roles/assign*") by Web.src Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where match(urls,"api_key") AND match(urls,"roles/assign")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.url) as urls min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/api/global/self/api_key*" OR Web.url="*/api/public/v1/roles/assign*") by Web.src Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where match(urls,"api_key") AND match(urls,"roles/assign")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Package-manager supply-chain control bypass via pnpm minimumReleaseAge=0 AIInstallation High
Hunts for npm/pnpm/yarn install invocations that explicitly set minimumReleaseAge=0 on the command line, disabling pnpm 11's default new-package quarantine window. This is the exact bypass the article cites (an AI coding agent running `pnpm install --config.minimumReleaseAge=0`), which re-opens the exposure window during which freshly published malicious packages are most dangerous. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim code block `pnpm install --config.minimumReleaseAge=0`; the value `=0` is the high-fidelity discriminator (legitimate hardening sets a positive minute count like 1440/10080, never 0). Cross-checked against pnpm's own supply-chain docs and a pnpm 11 write-up confirming 1440-minute default and that 0 disables the control. Cross-checked against: • https://pnpm.io/supply-chain-security • https://cybersecuritynews.com/pnpm-11-turns-on-minimum-release-age/ • https://pnpm.io/settings
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD build agent deliberately running with minimumReleaseAge=0 to always resolve latest dependencies
  • Developer pulling a legitimate security hotfix published inside the quarantine window
  • AI coding agent self-unblocking on a needed dependency (the article's own sanctioned-but-risky scenario)
  • Container image build step that bootstraps a monorepo and disables the delay for speed
  • Internal package-publish smoke tests that install their own just-published artifact
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line, parent process, and user/host. Determine if it ran under an interactive developer session or a CI/build agent, and whether the install pulled any package published within the last 24h. 2) Contain: if non-sanctioned, kill the install, quarantine the host's node_modules/lockfile delta, and block the resolved package versions pending review; require minimumReleaseAge to remain at the org default. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for newly installed packages (FileWritten under node_modules), outbound connections from node.exe to non-registry domains, and any postinstall script execution (node/npm spawning cmd/powershell) in the minutes after install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "minimumReleaseAge"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)minimumReleaseAge\s*=\s*0(\D|$)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "minimumReleaseAge"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)minimumReleaseAge\s*=\s*0(\D|$)"
| where not(Account endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:

    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or SHA1 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or MD5 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or SHA1 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or MD5 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — A tale of two eras
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Talos most-prevalent CoinMiner / W32.Injector / Win.Dropper.Miner file-hash watchlist · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Talos most-prevalent CoinMiner / W32.Injector / Win.Dropper.Miner file-hash watchlist AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution or on-disk drop of the four specific malware binaries Talos flagged as most-prevalent this week (Win.Worm.Coinminer 'VID001.exe', W32.Injector:Gen.21ie, Win.Dropper.Miner) by exact SHA256/MD5. Article-specific because it pins the named hashes from the Talos telemetry block rather than a generic miner/injector behaviour. Rationale: Pins the exact SHA256/MD5 pairs Talos published as most-prevalent (CoinMiner 'VID001.exe' 9f1f..., W32.Injector 96fa..., Win.Dropper.Miner a31f..., dropper 9896...). Hash-exact match is the only article-specific high-fidelity signal available; the article carries no command-lines or process trees. Cross-checked against Hybrid Analysis sandbox report and CIS Top 10 Malware before shipping. Cross-checked against: • https://hybrid-analysis.com/sample/9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507 • https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/top-10-malware-q4-2025 • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/a-tale-of-two-eras/
ATT&CKT1496 T1055.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis / detonation VM where a researcher intentionally ran the sample (sandbox host)
  • EDR or AV quarantine copy of the file being written to a vault path, re-firing the file-write branch
  • Threat-intel ingestion tooling that stages known-bad samples to disk for YARA/hash enrichment
  • IR collection host where the sample was copied off a victim for examination
  • Vulnerable-by-design / red-team lab images that purposely host prevalent malware corpora
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("SANDBOX01","MALWARE-ANALYSIS","IR-VAULT") and FolderPath !has @"\Quarantine\" and FolderPath !has @"\AV_Quarantine\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the DeviceName/aid is a production endpoint, not a sandbox or IR analysis host; pull the FolderPath, initiating process and signing status, and check whether it was ProcessCreated (executed) vs only dropped. Step 2 (contain): If executed on a production host, network-isolate the device via Defender/Falcon, kill and quarantine the binary, and capture the parent process for the delivery vector. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same SHA256/MD5 org-wide, then check for CoinMiner follow-on — high sustained CPU, outbound stratum/mining-pool connections, and WMI Event Consumer persistence — and for injector activity look for the dropped child under the same logon session.

(DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in~ (BadSHA256) or MD5 in~ (BadMD5) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Action = "ProcessCreated", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName),
(DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in~ (BadSHA256) or MD5 in~ (BadMD5) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, Action = ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadSHA256 = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91","9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f"]);

(ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadSHA256) or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadMD5) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Action = EventType, ActingProcessName, SHA256 = TargetFileSHA256, MD5 = TargetFileMD5, ActingProcessCommandLine)

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:

    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution

status: experimental

    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PHP runtime or web server spawning a shell/LOLBin (CodeIgniter webshell RCE)
CodeIgniter4 ext_in bypass: PHP-extension file written into web-accessible upload dir AIInstallation High
Hunts the artifact of CVE-2026-48062: a file with a PHP-executable extension (shell.php, .phtml, .phar) written by a PHP runtime or web-server process into an uploads/avatar/writable directory. The ext_in bypass lets GIF-content-but-.php-named files survive validation and land via $file->move($path) under the web root. Rationale: Anchored on the CVE-2026-48062 bypass artifact: $file->move($path) preserving a client-supplied PHP extension (shell.php) in CodeIgniter's web-accessible upload paths (uploads/avatar/writable named in the advisory workarounds), written specifically by a PHP/web-server process. Cross-checked GitLab advisory and CodeIgniter GitHub security advisories (fix v4.7.3, CWE-434). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/codeigniter4/framework/CVE-2026-48062/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2gr4-ppc7-7mhx • https://github.com/codeigniter4/CodeIgniter4/security/advisories
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CodeIgniter/Composer writing compiled PHP view/cache files (.php) under writable/cache during legitimate operation
  • Admin-initiated CMS/plugin/theme upload that legitimately deploys .php templates into the web root
  • Application self-update or artisan/spark commands generating PHP files under public/
  • Backup or staging tooling copying a full PHP app tree into wwwroot/htdocs
  • Developer deploying code via a web-based file manager
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "writable\\cache" or FileName startswith "ci_session") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("composer","spark","artisan"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the dropped file (FolderPath/SHA256) — confirm it is a single user-uploaded .php in an uploads/avatar dir (not framework cache); inspect contents for GIF magic header + PHP tags (<?php, eval, system, base64_decode) confirming the polyglot bypass. 2) Contain: quarantine/remove the file, revoke web-server execute permission on the upload directory, and block the uploading source IP at the WAF; isolate the host if the file already executed. 3) Hunt: pull the web logs for GET/POST to that exact path (UC2), check for php/php-cgi spawning shells (UC3), and verify the CodeIgniter4 version — anything <4.7.3 is vulnerable; review the app's upload validation chain for reliance on ext_in.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".phar" or FileName endswith ".pht" or FileName endswith ".phps" or FileName endswith ".php5" or FileName endswith ".php7"
| where FolderPath has_any ("uploads","avatar","writable","wwwroot","htdocs","public","www")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","httpd.exe","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php" or TargetFileName endswith ".phtml" or TargetFileName endswith ".phar" or TargetFileName endswith ".pht" or TargetFileName endswith ".phps"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("uploads","avatar","writable","wwwroot","htdocs","public")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","httpd","apache","nginx","w3wp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, DvcAction, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PHP-Executable File Written to Web-Accessible Upload Directory (CVE-2026-48062)
id: 6f4c2b1e-9a3d-4e21-8b77-2c1f0a9d5e44
description: Detects a PHP-executable file written by a PHP runtime or web server into an uploads/writable directory, the artifact of the CodeIgniter4 ext_in upload validation bypass (CVE-2026-48062).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2gr4-ppc7-7mhx
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/codeigniter4/framework/CVE-2026-48062/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/26
tags:
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.php'
      - '.phtml'
      - '.phar'
      - '.pht'
      - '.phps'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\uploads\'
      - '\avatar'
      - '\writable\'
      - '\wwwroot\'
      - '\htdocs\'
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\php.exe'
      - '\php-cgi.exe'
      - '\httpd.exe'
      - '\nginx.exe'
      - '\w3wp.exe'
  condition: all of selection_*
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*.php OR *.PHP OR *.phtml OR *.phar OR *.pht OR *.phps)) (@TargetFilename:(*uploads* OR *Uploads* OR *avatar* OR *writable* OR *wwwroot* OR *htdocs*)) @Image:(*\php.exe OR *\php-cgi.exe OR *\PHP-CGI.EXE OR *\httpd.exe OR *\nginx.exe OR *\w3wp.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\.(php|phtml|phar|pht|phps|php5|php7)$/i
| regex("(uploads|avatar|writable|wwwroot|htdocs|/public/)", field=TargetFileName)
| ContextImageFileName=/(php|php-cgi|php-fpm|httpd|apache2|nginx|w3wp)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Webshell access: HTTP request to a .php file under a CodeIgniter upload/avatar path AICommand & Control Medium
Detects HTTP requests that successfully retrieve/execute a PHP file living under an uploads, avatar or writable directory — i.e. invocation of a webshell planted via the CVE-2026-48062 ext_in bypass. Legitimate CodeIgniter routes funnel through index.php, so a directly-served .php under an upload path is highly abnormal. Rationale: Uses the advisory's specific upload directories (uploads/writable) plus the avatar field from the documented vulnerable rule string; in a CodeIgniter4 app all routing goes through index.php, so a 200 on a .php served directly from an upload path is a strong webshell-invocation signal. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty: inbound HTTP URI telemetry is not present in EDR/FDR — this detection lives in web-server logs only. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/codeigniter4/framework/CVE-2026-48062/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2gr4-ppc7-7mhx
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legacy/non-CodeIgniter app on the same host that legitimately serves .php from a gallery or /images/ path (e.g. a thumbnailer script)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Acunetix) probing upload paths for .php and receiving 200 from a benign placeholder
  • Rewrite rules that map /uploads/<x>.php through to index.php returning 200 for a non-existent file
  • Legitimate file-manager plugin that stores and serves editable .php snippets
  • Monitoring/uptime checks hitting a known .php health endpoint under a public path
Suppression filter
| where not (csUserAgent has_any ("Nessus","Acunetix","nmap","masscan","Nuclei")) and csUriStem !endswith "/index.php"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the exact csUriStem and check whether that .php file exists on disk under the upload dir (correlate with UC1) and whether it was recently created; review csUserAgent and cIP for scanner vs interactive-shell patterns and look at csUriQuery for command params (cmd=, c=, exec=). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, remove the file, and disable execution in the upload directory (deny handler / php_admin_flag engine off). 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct .php under upload paths accessed in the window, pivot to host process telemetry (UC3) for php/php-cgi spawning shells, and review all source IPs that touched the same file for lateral access.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem endswith ".php" or csUriStem endswith ".phtml" or csUriStem endswith ".phar" or csUriStem endswith ".pht"
| where csUriStem has_any ("/uploads/","/avatar","/writable/","/images/")
| where scStatus == 200
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, csUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PHP runtime or web server spawning a shell/LOLBin (CodeIgniter webshell RCE) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a PHP interpreter or web-server process (php-cgi, php-fpm, httpd, nginx) spawning a command shell or recon/download LOLBin — the post-exploitation execution that follows a webshell dropped via the CVE-2026-48062 ext_in bypass. PHP runtimes legitimately almost never spawn cmd/powershell/bash/whoami. Rationale: Targets the RCE consequence of the bypass: a webshell's PHP code calling system()/exec(), which manifests as php-cgi/php-fpm/httpd as parent of cmd/powershell/sh/whoami. Parent set is restricted to PHP/web runtimes (w3wp deliberately excluded) so the parent->child pair is inherently high-fidelity for the CodeIgniter RCE chain described in the advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/codeigniter4/framework/CVE-2026-48062/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2gr4-ppc7-7mhx
ATT&CKT1059 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP app legitimately shelling out to ImageMagick/ffmpeg via system() for avatar/thumbnail processing (often invokes sh -c)
  • Composer/Laravel/CI scheduled jobs (spark/cron) spawning git, curl or php subprocesses for deploy or webhook delivery
  • PHP-based monitoring/health scripts running whoami or net to report context
  • CI/CD agent running under php-fpm invoking build tooling
  • Legitimate admin plugin offering a 'system info' page that calls uname/whoami
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","ffmpeg","imagemagick","gs ","/usr/bin/git") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("spark","artisan","composer"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine of the child and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine of the PHP parent; benign image-processing calls reference convert/ffmpeg with file paths, whereas whoami/net/curl-to-external or interactive cmd are malicious — confirm the PHP working directory is an upload path. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and pull execute permissions on the upload directory; preserve the parent PHP script for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the dropped file (UC1) and webshell access logs (UC2), search for follow-on persistence/credential access from the same host, and confirm CodeIgniter4 is patched to >=4.7.3.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","httpd.exe","apache2","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","whoami.exe","whoami","net.exe","net1.exe","curl.exe","curl","wget","certutil.exe","python.exe","python3")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php","php-cgi","php-fpm","httpd","apache","nginx")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","/bin/sh","bash","dash","whoami","net.exe","curl","wget","certutil","python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — npm v12 delivers one of the biggest security improvements in years
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] axios RAT Windows payload drop (6202033.vbs/.ps1, ProgramData\wt) during npm install · [LLM] Shai-Hulud npm preinstall Bun bootstrap (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] axios npm RAT C2 beacon to UNC1069 infra (142.11.206.73 / sfrclak.com) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TruffleHog secret-scan spawned by npm/node install (Shai-Hulud credential harvest) · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
axios npm RAT C2 beacon to UNC1069 infra (142.11.206.73 / sfrclak.com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections to the hard-coded command-and-control infrastructure used by the March 2026 axios/plain-crypto-js supply-chain RAT (UNC1069). Any internal host reaching 142.11.206.73 or resolving sfrclak.com after an npm install is a confirmed post-install RAT beacon. Rationale: Anchors on the dedicated C2 IP 142.11.206.73 and domain sfrclak.com, confirmed by Google Threat Intelligence, Microsoft and SANS as UNC1069's axios-campaign infrastructure (port 8000, 60s beacon) — a pure IOC match with effectively no benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/north-korea-threat-actor-targets-axios-npm-package • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.sans.org/blog/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise-malicious-packages-remote-access-trojan
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating the axios sample in a malware sandbox that egresses to the live C2
  • Threat-intel enrichment/scanning tooling actively connecting to the IOC IP to fingerprint it
  • Internal honeypot or deception host deliberately reaching the IOC
  • IP later reassigned to a benign hosting provider months after takedown
  • Proxy log replays / SIEM test harness injecting the IOC for rule validation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the source host and the initiating process for the connection (DeviceNetworkEvents InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine); confirm an npm/node install ran in the prior minutes. Step 2 (contain): Network-isolate the host, block 142.11.206.73 and sfrclak.com at egress, and kill the beaconing process tree. Step 3 (hunt): Search the same host for %TEMP%\6202033.vbs/.ps1 and %PROGRAMDATA%\wt drops, enumerate installed package-lock for axios@1.14.1/0.30.4 and plain-crypto-js@4.2.1, and rotate any npm/SSH/cloud tokens present on the host.

| where RemoteIP == "142.11.206.73" or RemoteUrl has "sfrclak.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "142.11.206.73" or DestinationHostName has "sfrclak.com" or RequestURL has "sfrclak.com"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

axios RAT Windows payload drop (6202033.vbs/.ps1, ProgramData\wt) during npm install AIInstallation High
Hunts the Windows-specific payload files written by the March 2026 axios supply-chain RAT — %TEMP%\6202033.vbs, %TEMP%\6202033.ps1 and the %PROGRAMDATA%\wt staging dir — plus the campaign's malware SHA256 set. Surfaces the install-time RAT drop before C2 is established. Rationale: Uses the exact Windows artifact names (6202033.vbs/.ps1, %PROGRAMDATA%\wt) documented by SANS/Microsoft plus the article's pre-extracted SHA256 set; file names + hashes are high-fidelity and effectively never collide with benign software. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sans.org/blog/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise-malicious-packages-remote-access-trojan • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://snyk.io/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised-supply-chain-attack-delivers-cross-platform/

  • Windows Terminal or other vendor unpacking a benign 'wt' folder under ProgramData (path clause only)
  • DFIR analyst copying the captured sample onto an investigation host

Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, quarantine the dropped files, and kill any wscript/powershell process executing 6202033.vbs/.ps1. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for 142.11.206.73/sfrclak.com from the same host, check %PROGRAMDATA%\wt for the persistent RAT binary and any scheduled task/Run key pointing at it, and audit the project's package-lock for axios@1.14.1/0.30.4 and plain-crypto-js@4.2.1.

Shai-Hulud npm preinstall Bun bootstrap (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Shai-Hulud 2.0 / Mini Shai-Hulud worm bootstrap: an npm lifecycle script invoking node against setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js / bun_installer.js / environment_source.js, or a Bun runtime spawned as a child of node/npm. Bun appearing inside a Node install is the campaign's signature anomaly. Rationale: Anchors on the exact Shai-Hulud preinstall script filenames confirmed by Datadog/ReversingLabs/Zscaler plus the anomalous 'bun spawned by node/npm' relationship the worm relies on to evade Node-focused defenses. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/shai-hulud-worm-npm • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/shai-hulud-v2-poses-risk-npm-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A team that legitimately uses the Bun runtime in a Node monorepo (e.g. TanStack tooling) invoking bun via node wrappers
  • A developer who genuinely named a setup helper setup_bun.js for a real Bun migration
  • CI agents bootstrapping Bun as part of a sanctioned toolchain
  • Container image builds that install Bun under node during npm/pnpm steps
  • Local benchmarking comparing Bun vs Node started from an npm script
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("tanstack","bunfig.toml") or FolderPath has @"\.bun\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent npm install — confirm the script came from node_modules (a dependency) rather than the repo's own committed tooling. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the bun/node tree, and freeze the developer's npm and GitHub tokens. Step 3 (hunt): Look on the same host for TruffleHog execution, outbound pushes to attacker GitHub repos, and any newly-published packages from the maintainer's account; scan node_modules for setup_bun.js/bun_environment.js to scope the blast radius.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js","bun_installer.js","environment_source.js")
   or (FileName =~ "bun.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","cmd.exe"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js","bun_installer.js","environment_source.js")
   or (ActingProcessName has "bun" and ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TruffleHog secret-scan spawned by npm/node install (Shai-Hulud credential harvest) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts TruffleHog being executed as a child of node/npm/bun — the Shai-Hulud worm's credential-harvesting step that sweeps SSH keys, GitHub/npm tokens and cloud credentials during install. TruffleHog launched by a package manager (rather than CI/pre-commit) is the article-specific signal. Rationale: Anchors on TruffleHog (the Shai-Hulud secret-sweeper named by Datadog/ReversingLabs) constrained to a node/npm/bun parent, distinguishing worm-driven credential theft from sanctioned CI/pre-commit secret scanning. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/shai-hulud-worm-npm
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A husky/lint-staged pre-commit hook running TruffleHog as a child of node (legitimate secret scanning)
  • A developer manually running trufflehog via an npm script for a security review
  • CI runners executing TruffleHog through a Node-based pipeline wrapper
  • Security tooling that wraps TruffleHog in a node CLI installed org-wide
  • A package that legitimately vendors TruffleHog for its own scanning feature
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("husky","lint-staged","pre-commit",".git/hooks"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine whether the trufflehog invocation originated from a committed dev hook (husky/lint-staged in the repo) or from inside node_modules / a lifecycle script — the latter is malicious. Step 2 (contain): If unsanctioned, isolate the host, kill the process tree, and immediately rotate all secrets reachable from that workstation (SSH keys, GitHub/npm/cloud tokens). Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with Bun bootstrap scripts (setup_bun.js) and outbound activity to attacker-controlled GitHub repos or 142.11.206.73/sfrclak.com on the same host, and review the maintainer's recent npm publishes for worm propagation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "trufflehog" or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","bun.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","sh.exe","bash.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "trufflehog" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm","bun","cmd","powershell","sh","bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Unauthenticated MCP tool invocation: external POST /mcp to Meta Ads MCP server (CVE-2026-48039) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POST requests to the Streamable-HTTP MCP `/mcp` endpoint from non-internal source IPs, captured in proxy/WAF/web-server logs. CVE-2026-48039 lets any network-reachable caller invoke MCP tools without auth because AuthInjectionMiddleware.dispatch() never returns 401; an MCP server that should be loopback-only being POSTed from a public source is the exploit signal. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete exploit endpoint (POST /mcp, default port 8080) plus a public-source-IP constraint to flag external reach to a server meant to be loopback-bound. defender_kql/datadog/falcon are empty because Defender XDR and FDR do not ingest arbitrary Python web-server request logs and there is no generic HTTP source in this Datadog tenant — the detection lives in proxy/WAF/IIS telemetry. Corroborated against the repo's Streamable-HTTP setup docs confirming the /mcp + JSON-RPC transport. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp/blob/main/STREAMABLE_HTTP_SETUP.md • https://chatforest.com/builders-log/mcp-security-crisis-2026-unauthenticated-servers-viper-nsa-owasp-builder-guide/
ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal MCP client (Claude Desktop / pipeboard connector) reaching the server via a NAT/proxy that rewrites the source to a public-looking egress IP
  • Authorized external SaaS integration or remote operator intentionally calling the hosted MCP at mcp.pipeboard.co
  • Security scanner / ASM tooling probing /mcp during an authorized assessment
  • Load balancer or CDN health checks hitting /mcp from an external VIP
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "health" and SourceIP !in ("<corp egress IPs managed via watchlist>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination host is a meta-ads-mcp instance and whether it is intended to be internet-exposed; pull the full request and check whether an Authorization/X-META-ACCESS-TOKEN header was present. Note the source IP and geo. 2) Contain: firewall the MCP port (8080) to loopback/internal only, upgrade past meta-ads-mcp 1.0.108, and rotate the META_ACCESS_TOKEN since exposure must be assumed. 3) Hunt: review proxy logs for any response/outbound URL containing access_token= (UC3) and for Meta Graph API activity from unfamiliar IPs after the request window.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/mcp"
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false   // MCP /mcp endpoint should never be reachable from a public/non-internal source
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

External inbound connection to Meta Ads MCP listener on default port 8080 AIDelivery Medium
Detects public/external inbound TCP connections accepted on local port 8080 by a Python-hosted Meta Ads MCP server. CVE-2026-48039 requires only network reachability to the MCP HTTP port; an unauthenticated attacker reaching the default 8080 listener from a public address is the pre-exploitation network signal for shops with EDR network telemetry but no web logs. Rationale: Pivots on the article's default listener port (8080) and the Python MCP server process, scoped to public inbound only so it surfaces the network-reachability precondition of CVE-2026-48039 from EDR telemetry alone. Sigma omitted because inbound-listener semantics don't map cleanly to a single Sysmon network_connection selection. Datadog/CloudWatch empty as the host is a Linux/container Python service not shipping inbound-port fields here. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp/blob/main/STREAMABLE_HTTP_SETUP.md
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote MCP client connecting to an intentionally-exposed self-hosted instance
  • Internal vulnerability scanner / ASM service connecting to 8080 from a management subnet that appears public
  • Reverse-proxy or container host NAT presenting the upstream connection with a public RemoteIP
  • Another unrelated service legitimately bound to 8080 on the same host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp","meta-ads-mcp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the listening process is meta-ads-mcp (check InitiatingProcessCommandLine for meta_ads_mcp/streamable-http) and whether the host is meant to be internet-facing; correlate the RemoteIP against known clients. 2) Contain: restrict 8080 to localhost/internal CIDRs via host firewall, upgrade past 1.0.108, and rotate META_ACCESS_TOKEN. 3) Hunt: cross-reference the same RemoteIP in proxy logs for POST /mcp (UC1) and for any graph.facebook.com URLs leaking access_token= (UC3).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8080
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "python" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("uvicorn.exe","pythonw.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp","meta-ads-mcp","streamable-http")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber == 8080
| where NetworkDirection == "Inbound"
| where ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr) == false
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 LocalPort=8080
| ContextImageFileName=/python|uvicorn/i

Meta Graph API access token exposed in URL query string (meta-ads-mcp token leak) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts proxy/web-log URLs to graph.facebook.com that carry the operator credential as an `access_token=` query parameter. CVE-2026-48039's impact is that meta-ads-mcp appends access_token to the Graph API URL (api.py:136) and reflects it in error responses, so any long-lived Meta token appearing in URL logs is a recoverable credential exposure. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's leak mechanism (api.py:136 appends access_token to the graph.facebook.com URL, reflected in error responses) — any URL log line with graph.facebook.com + access_token= is a recoverable long-lived credential. High FP/exposure-hunt by nature since the buggy app emits this on every call; that is exactly the hygiene finding. Defender/Falcon empty because EDR RemoteUrl is host-only and never captures the query string; no AWS/Datadog HTTP source applies. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/pipeboard-co/meta-ads-mcp/blob/main/STREAMABLE_HTTP_SETUP.md • https://pipeboard.co/guides/api-token-permissions
ATT&CKT1552 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal (but insecure) meta-ads-mcp operation emitting access_token in every Graph API URL — expected volume, still a real exposure
  • Other legitimate apps/scripts that authenticate to Graph API via URL token rather than Authorization header
  • Developer/debug traffic or Postman calls to graph.facebook.com during integration testing
  • Proxy SSL-inspection logging full URLs for sanctioned marketing tools
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the captured access_token belongs to the org's Meta Ads operator account and over what window/IPs it appeared in URL logs; treat any token seen in logs as compromised. 2) Contain: rotate/invalidate the META_ACCESS_TOKEN in Meta Business settings, upgrade meta-ads-mcp past 1.0.108, and reconfigure the client to send the token via Authorization: Bearer header (not URL). 3) Hunt: review Meta Ads account audit logs and Graph API usage for actions from unrecognized IPs after first exposure, and correlate with UC1/UC2 inbound exploitation against the MCP host.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "graph.facebook.com"
| where RequestURL has "access_token="
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
SPECTRALVIPER DLL side-load: IntelAudioService.exe (renamed dtlupdate.exe) loads DtlCrashCatch.dll AIInstallation High
Hunts the OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER side-load chain where a renamed legitimate signed binary (dtlupdate.exe masquerading as IntelAudioService.exe) loads the malicious DtlCrashCatch.dll loader. Article-specific because both the masqueraded EXE name and the unique malicious DLL name are named IOCs from the FireAnt MetaKit campaign. Rationale: DtlCrashCatch.dll and the dtlupdate.exe→IntelAudioService.exe masquerade are named in the cybersecuritynews/gbhackers write-ups of the FireAnt SPECTRALVIPER chain; the DLL name is unique enough that any load/write is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/oceanlotus-apt-compromises-fireant-metakit/ • https://gbhackers.com/oceanlotus-targets-stock-investors/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named Intel audio service binary loading an unrelated vendor DLL (the pair clause only — the DtlCrashCatch.dll clause has no benign match)
  • Security-vendor sandbox/detonation hosts replaying the sample
  • IR/forensics team copying the DLL onto an analysis VM triggering FileCreate
  • Backup/restore agent rehydrating quarantined files
Suppression filter
| where not (LoaderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Intel\\" and Module !~ "DtlCrashCatch.dll")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loader's path and signer — genuine Intel binaries live under Program Files\Intel; a DtlCrashCatch.dll under a user/Temp/AppData path is malicious. Pull the LoaderSHA1 and cross-check against the campaign hash list. 2) Contain: isolate the host in Defender/Falcon, kill the IntelAudioService.exe/dtlupdate.exe process tree, and quarantine DtlCrashCatch.dll. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe network egress and connections to financemachinelearning.com and the campaign C2 IPs; check whether setup.exe (FireAnt MetaKit updater) wrote the DLL.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "DtlCrashCatch.dll" or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "IntelAudioService.exe" and FileName endswith ".dll")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Loader=InitiatingProcessFileName, LoaderPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoaderSHA1=InitiatingProcessSHA1, Module=FileName, ModulePath=FolderPath, ModuleSHA1=SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "DtlCrashCatch.dll"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA1, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
